Extension architecture

Summary. GoFish should own the middle of the pipeline (data types, composition, the scale and layout solve, and the display list) and let other libraries own the two ends: where data comes from and what draws the picture. A lonboard or fastplotlib program can then be written in GoFish style, with the domain package adding only what belongs to its domain.

Recommendation. Do two small things now, both on the display list that already exists: (1) make the engine a pure function with text measurement passed in, and (2) run that engine inside Python through an embedded JavaScript runtime. Both worked as throwaway prototypes. Hold the larger pieces (columns in the display list, open coords, registration of extension constructs) until the three forks below are settled. The two steps help GoFish's own Python users whether or not any other library ever builds on GoFish. Before building anything for a partner, fix the wall where one render has one set of scales, and build one visualization that crosses domains and that no single library can draw.

Status. Exploratory. Nothing here is signed off. The evidence is real: nine example programs rendered with today's GoFish, and a spike that ran the engine in Node and in Python and drew the result with matplotlib and pygfx.

Nine real programs from lonboard, fastplotlib and ProgressiVis were rewritten in GoFish style and rendered with today's GoFish (small data, SVG).

Lines marked # NEW or # PLANNED use names that do not exist yet.

How the examples were written

This page tests one requirement: a lonboard or fastplotlib program should be writable in GoFish style, with the same chart(...).flow(...).mark(...), layer, spread, color and legend machinery, and with the domain package adding only what is truly about its domain. Each section has the original program (copied from the library's own examples, with its URL), the GoFish-style program in Python and JS as a user of a future extension package would write it, a render of the nearest honest thing GoFish draws today, a table of who owns what, and the gaps.

Conventions used below:

  • gofish_geo / @gofish/geo, gofish_fpl / @gofish/fpl and gofish_progressive / @gofish/progressive are placeholder package names.
  • Every name that does not exist in GoFish today is marked # NEW: or // NEW:. A name marked # PLANNED: is one the docs already announce but that is not built (Domain.continuous).
  • The renders are the stories in packages/gofish-graphics/stories/_proposals/ExtensionArchitecture.stories.tsx, drawn with pnpm capture-one "extension architecture" and copied to img/ex-<id>.png. They use only public exports of src/lib.ts and small data. Where a render needed a workaround, the story says so in a comment that starts with "Workaround, declared", and the gaps list repeats it.
  • Data: L2 and L3 use real county geometry and migration flows (a Kansas, Nebraska and Colorado subset of deck.gl's counties.json, the data of lonboard's migration notebook). L1, L4, all of F and P1 use synthetic data, labeled as such in the data files and the stories.

The rules the rewrites follow: a coord appears only at a chart() or layer boundary; one by key; options nest instead of taking prefixes; Python passes children positionally and options as snake_case keywords; strategies are Family.member(); .name() appears only when something selects it.

lonboard

L1. Points colored by a continuous value (lonboard internet-speeds)

Story L1_SpeedPoints. 2,082 SYNTHETIC points on land in the notebook's window (fast near fifteen capitals), the clamp done in a derive, BrBG stops written out as a list, the basemap drawn as world110m country polygons. The colorbar comes for free. The radius is a constant 2 px: a radius from data under Coord.geo timed out (30 s) at this size, and at 1 px size it drew boxes, not circles (see walls).

GoFish style, Python

import geopandas as gpd
from palettable.colorbrewer.diverging import BrBG_10
from gofish import chart, layer, scatter, circle, Color, Coord, Unit, Domain
from gofish_geo import basemap  # NEW: a mark that draws map tiles
from gofish_geo import Painter  # NEW: family; Painter.deckgl comes from the geo package

gdf = gpd.read_parquet("internet-speeds.parquet").cx[-11.83:25.5, 34.9:59]

layer(
    [
        basemap("carto-positron"),  # NEW
        chart(
            gdf, schema={"avg_d_kbps": Unit(domain=Domain.continuous(5000, 50000))}
        )  # PLANNED: Domain.continuous
        .flow(scatter(at="geometry"))  # NEW option: place by a point-valued column
        .mark(circle(area="avg_d_kbps", fill="avg_d_kbps", opacity=0.7)),
    ],
    coord=Coord.geo("mercator"),
    color=Color.gradient(BrBG_10.hex_colors),
).render(
    h=800, painter=Painter.deckgl()
)  # NEW option + family member
The lonboard program

Source: https://github.com/developmentseed/lonboard/blob/main/examples/internet-speeds.ipynb (code cells, in order; the # /// script header is omitted). 

from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
import shapely
from palettable.colorbrewer.diverging import BrBG_10
from sidecar import Sidecar

from lonboard import Map, ScatterplotLayer
from lonboard.colormap import apply_continuous_cmap

url = "https://ookla-open-data.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/parquet/performance/type=mobile/year=2019/quarter=1/2019-01-01_performance_mobile_tiles.parquet"

local_path = Path("internet-speeds.parquet")
if local_path.exists():
    gdf = gpd.read_parquet(local_path)
else:
    columns = ["avg_d_kbps", "tile"]
    df = pd.read_parquet(url, columns=columns)

    tile_geometries = shapely.from_wkt(df["tile"])
    tile_centroids = shapely.centroid(tile_geometries)
    gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(df[["avg_d_kbps"]], geometry=tile_centroids, crs="EPSG:4326")
    gdf.to_parquet(local_path)

gdf.head()

gdf = gdf.cx[-11.83:25.5, 34.9:59]

gdf

sidecar = Sidecar(anchor="split-right")

layer = ScatterplotLayer.from_geopandas(gdf)
m = Map(layer, height=800)
with sidecar:
    display(m)

layer.get_fill_color = [0, 0, 200, 200]

min_bound = 5000
max_bound = 50000
download_speed = gdf["avg_d_kbps"]
normalized_download_speed = (download_speed - min_bound) / (max_bound - min_bound)

normalized_download_speed

BrBG_10.mpl_colormap

layer.get_fill_color = apply_continuous_cmap(
    normalized_download_speed,
    BrBG_10,
    alpha=0.7,
)

layer.get_radius = normalized_download_speed * 200
layer.radius_units = "meters"
layer.radius_min_pixels = 0.5
GoFish style, JS 
import {
  chart,
  layer,
  scatter,
  circle,
  Color,
  Coord,
  Unit,
  Domain,
} from "gofish-graphics";
import { basemap, Painter } from "@gofish/geo"; // NEW: basemap (mark), Painter (family)
import { readParquet } from "@gofish/geo"; // NEW: a GeoArrow table source

const tiles = await readParquet("internet-speeds.parquet");

layer(
  [
    basemap("carto-positron"), // NEW
    chart(tiles, {
      schema: { avg_d_kbps: Unit({ domain: Domain.continuous(5000, 50000) }) },
    }) // PLANNED
      .flow(scatter({ at: "geometry" })) // NEW option
      .mark(circle({ area: "avg_d_kbps", fill: "avg_d_kbps", opacity: 0.7 })),
  ],
  { coord: Coord.geo("mercator"), color: Color.gradient(BrBG_10) }
).render(container, { h: 800, painter: Painter.deckgl() }); // NEW
Notes on the rewrite

What changed against lonboard: the normalization to [5000, 50000] and the colormap call become one declaration on the data (the unit's domain) and one color scale, and the legend follows from them. radius_units = "meters" and radius_min_pixels become circle({ area }), so the size is a value with a size legend rather than a distance on the ground. If a user really wants a ground distance, the spelling is a length unit on the column, which the geo coord would turn into pixels (Unit("m")); that is a gap, below.

The hand normalization and the colormap call become one declared domain and one color scale, and the colorbar follows from them. lonboard has no legend at all (lonboard issue 492: its author does not want to provide an on-map colormap legend).

Fork: where the painter is chosen

(a) An option of .render(...): painter: Painter.deckgl(). The spec is the same object whether it is drawn as SVG in the docs or by deck.gl in a notebook, and Python and JS take the same option. Cost: the user has to know a painter exists when the data is large.

(b) Inferred: the engine picks WebGL above some row count. Cost: a heuristic users have to model, which the project has ruled out (an explicit default plus an override is the rule).

(c) A property of a mark (circle(...).painter(...)). Cost: two painters in one picture must agree on the canvas, z-order and hit testing, and the spec now says how, not what.

Lean (a), with SVG as the written default, and with the painter free to hand items it cannot draw (text, for example) to SVG above it. The measured numbers from the scaling proposal make the case: 1e6 circles take 9.3 s in GoFish's SVG painter and 35 ms in WebGL.

Fork: how a basemap enters

(a) A mark in the layer, first in paint order: basemap("carto-positron"). It needs the final window and zoom, so it elaborates late, like an axis: it desugars to an image per tile whose rows come from a tile source that reads the view. It can be reordered (lonboard's interleaved-labels example puts labels above data), hidden, or left out.

(b) A property of the coord (Coord.geo("mercator", { basemap })). Cost: a coord is a transform, and this makes it draw; it also cannot put labels above data.

(c) A render option. Cost: the same, plus it does not round-trip with the spec.

Lean (a).

Fork: projection and CRS

Coord.geo exists and takes a projection name or a function. The geo package adds only values: an EPSG code (Coord.geo("EPSG:3857"), through proj4 / pyproj), and it reads the data's own CRS from the geometry column's type, so a GeoDataFrame in EPSG:4326 and one in a UTM zone both land in the same map without a to_crs call. No new coord name. Lonboard's maps are always Web Mercator, which is Coord.geo("mercator") today.

Fork: a point-valued column

(a) scatter({ at: "geometry" }): one new option, a channel whose value is a point, which the same option also serves for fastplotlib's (n, 2) arrays (F2). Precedent: deck.gl's getPosition, Observable Plot's geo mark and centroid transform.

(b) Two field methods, scatter({ x: field("geometry").x(), y: field("geometry").y() }), which fit the rule that a method reads the caller's type and can fail loudly on a non-point type. Cost: longer, and it splits one value into two channels.

Lean (a).

Who owns what

The geo package still owns GoFish gives it
Reading GeoParquet / GeoArrow, the geometry column type and its CRS The color scale, the colorbar legend, a size legend for area
Tile basemaps (basemap, the tile source behind it) The projection fit to the box, the window, aspect ratio
The deck.gl painter for 1e6 points Layering with any other GoFish visualization, axes when wanted
Lengths on the ground (meters) under a projection selectAll over the points, labels, Python/JS parity

Gaps

  • No tile basemap. Missing: a basemap mark over a tile source that reads the view. Slots: source and mark. The render uses world110m polygons.
  • 1e6 points is out of reach for the SVG painter. Slot: painter.
  • A data-valued radius under Coord.geo is slow (timeout at 2,082 points) and draws boxes, because the size is projected as a data-space box. Slot: coord (the geo coord must map a length at a point, and keep a circle round).
  • No continuous domain to clamp a color scale to. Domain.continuous is announced in the Domain family but not built. Slot: data type.
  • Polygons that cross the window's edge are not clipped (Spain and Russia spill out to the right, under the legend). Slot: core (a coord window should clip), not the extension.
  • Point geometry is two columns today (lon, lat). Slot: data type plus the at option.

L2. Choropleth (lonboard kontur population)

Story L2_Choropleth. GoFish has no H3 type, so this is the nearest honest choropleth: real county polygons (Kansas, Nebraska, Colorado) filled by real net migration from the same data as L3, with BrBG clipped to ±1,500 in a derive so the gradient's middle falls on 0. The colorbar comes for free.

GoFish style, Python

from gofish import chart, polygon, Color, Coord
from gofish_geo import H3  # NEW: data type, an H3 cell

# The log mapping (LogNorm) has no spelling yet; see the note below.

(
    chart(
        df,
        schema={"h3": H3()},
        coord=Coord.geo("mercator"),
        color=Color.gradient(BrBG_10.hex_colors),
    ).mark(polygon(points="h3", fill="population", opacity=0.7))
)
The lonboard program

Source: https://github.com/developmentseed/lonboard/blob/main/examples/kontur_pop.ipynb 

import warnings

import geopandas as gpd
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm
from palettable.colorbrewer.diverging import BrBG_10
from sidecar import Sidecar

from lonboard import H3HexagonLayer, Map
from lonboard.colormap import apply_continuous_cmap

url = "https://geodata-eu-central-1-kontur-public.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/kontur_datasets/kontur_population_20231101_r4.gpkg.gz"

# Wrap with GDAL's virtual file prefixes
vsipath = f"/vsigzip//vsicurl/{url}"

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.filterwarnings(
        "ignore",
        message="HTTP response code",
        category=RuntimeWarning,
    )
    gdf = gpd.read_file(vsipath, use_arrow=True)

df = gdf[["h3", "population"]]

pop = df["population"]
min_bound = pop.min()
max_bound = pop.max()
normalizer = LogNorm(min_bound, max_bound, clip=True)
normalized = normalizer(pop)

sidecar = Sidecar(anchor="split-right")

layer = H3HexagonLayer.from_pandas(
    df,
    get_hexagon=df["h3"],
    get_fill_color=apply_continuous_cmap(normalized, BrBG_10, alpha=0.7),
)
m = Map(layer)
with sidecar:
    display(m)
GoFish style, JS 
import { chart, polygon, Color, Coord } from "gofish-graphics";
import { H3 } from "@gofish/geo"; // NEW: data type

chart(df, {
  schema: { h3: H3() },
  coord: Coord.geo("mercator"),
  color: Color.gradient(BrBG_10),
})
  .mark(polygon({ points: "h3", fill: "population", opacity: 0.7 }))
  .render(container);
Notes on the rewrite

The H3 cell is the clearest case of what a domain package should add: a column type. polygon({ points }) already reads a ring per row (the world basemap stories use it). An H3 type says "this string is a hexagon", gives polygon its boundary ring, gives scatter({ at }) its center, and could give Bin a member (Bin.h3({ resolution })) so raw points can be binned into H3 cells by the same partition the 2D histogram uses (P1). The log color mapping is LogNorm. GoFish has no log color scale today; the scale-transforms proposal moves transforms onto coords and a Transform family, which is not built. With no transform, the spelling today is a derive that takes the log.

Who owns what

The geo package still owns GoFish gives it
The H3 column type: boundary, center, binning member polygon, the gradient, the colorbar legend
Reading GeoPackage over HTTP The projection fit, layering with a basemap or other layers
(Large cell counts: the painter) Hover and selection over the cells (selectAll)

Gaps

  • No H3 (or any discrete global grid) cell type. Slot: data type.
  • No log color mapping and no gradient midpoint (Trait.diverging centers a stack, not a color scale). Slot: core (scale transforms), not the extension.
  • No hole support in polygon (world110m notes this shortcut too). Slot: core mark.

L3. Multi-layer map with brushing (lonboard migration)

Story L3_MultiLayer, real data. County polygons as the basemap, a ring per county colored by the sign of its net migration, filled source points and arcs inside 200 km of a brush frozen at Denver. The legend for in / out comes for free. Arcs are straight, one color, built as two endpoint rows per arc threaded with group + scatter + line (the Bird Migration idiom). The spelling above, resolve + line({ from, to }) against the named rings, draws its lines in the wrong place under Coord.geo. The picture is under the gaps.

GoFish style, Python

The arc-building loop above is data preparation and stays as plain Python (it builds arcs, sources and targets; GoFish does not want to own it). What changes is everything after it. Python has no interaction today, so the brush is a fixed one-row dataset here. 

from gofish import (
    chart,
    scatter,
    circle,
    line,
    polygon,
    resolve,
    select_all,
    filter,
    Color,
    Coord,
    Curve,
)
from gofish_geo import (
    within_km,
)  # NEW: data helper, a distance predicate on point columns

brush = [{"geometry": Point(-104.99, 39.74)}]  # the pointer, frozen

(
    chart(
        counties_gdf,
        coord=Coord.geo("mercator"),
        color=Color.palette({"out": "rgb(166,3,3)", "in": "rgb(35,181,184)"}),
    )
    .mark(polygon(points="geometry", fill="#f3f3f3", stroke="#d0d0d0"))
    .layer(
        chart(target_gdf)
        .flow(scatter(by="name", at="geometry"))  # NEW option at
        .mark(circle(r=3, fill="none", stroke="direction").name("counties"))
    )
    .layer(
        chart(source_gdf)
        .flow(filter(within_km("geometry", brush, 200)), scatter(at="geometry"))
        .mark(circle(r=2, fill="direction"))
    )
    .layer(
        chart(arcs_df)
        .flow(
            filter(within_km(["source", "target"], brush, 200)),
            resolve(["source", "target"], from_=select_all("counties")),
        )
        .mark(
            line(
                from_="source",
                to="target",
                stroke="direction",
                opacity=0.4,
                curve=Curve.geodesic(),
            )
        )  # NEW member
    )
)
The lonboard program

Source: https://github.com/developmentseed/lonboard/blob/main/examples/migration.ipynb (polygons are not in this notebook; it layers points, rings and arcs. The GoFish version adds the county polygons as its basemap, which makes it polygons + paths + points.) 

import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa
import requests
import shapely
from matplotlib.colors import Normalize

from lonboard import ArcLayer, Map, ScatterplotLayer
from lonboard.layer_extension import BrushingExtension

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/visgl/deck.gl-data/master/examples/arc/counties.json"
r = requests.get(url)
source_data = r.json()

arcs = []
targets = []
sources = []
pairs = {}

features = source_data["features"]
for i, county in enumerate(features):
    flows = county["properties"]["flows"]
    target_centroid = county["properties"]["centroid"]
    total_value = {
        "gain": 0,
        "loss": 0,
    }

    for to_id, value in flows.items():
        if value > 0:
            total_value["gain"] += value
        else:
            total_value["loss"] += value

        # If number is too small, ignore it
        if abs(value) < 50:
            continue

        pair_key = "-".join(map(str, sorted([i, int(to_id)])))
        source_centroid = features[int(to_id)]["properties"]["centroid"]
        gain = np.sign(value)

        # add point at arc source
        sources.append(
            {
                "position": source_centroid,
                "target": target_centroid,
                "name": features[int(to_id)]["properties"]["name"],
                "radius": 3,
                "gain": -gain,
            },
        )
        # eliminate duplicate arcs
        if pair_key in pairs:
            continue

        pairs[pair_key] = True

        if gain > 0:
            arcs.append(
                {
                    "target": target_centroid,
                    "source": source_centroid,
                    "value": value,
                },
            )
        else:
            arcs.append(
                {
                    "target": source_centroid,
                    "source": target_centroid,
                    "value": value,
                },
            )

    # add point at arc target
    targets.append(
        {
            **total_value,
            "position": [target_centroid[0], target_centroid[1], 10],
            "net": total_value["gain"] + total_value["loss"],
            "name": county["properties"]["name"],
        },
    )

# sort targets by radius large -> small
targets = sorted(targets, key=lambda d: abs(d["net"]), reverse=True)
normalizer = Normalize(0, abs(targets[0]["net"]))

# migrate out
SOURCE_COLOR = [166, 3, 3]
# migrate in
TARGET_COLOR = [35, 181, 184]
# Combine into a single arr to use as a lookup table
COLORS = np.vstack(
    [np.array(SOURCE_COLOR, dtype=np.uint8), np.array(TARGET_COLOR, dtype=np.uint8)],
)
SOURCE_LOOKUP = 0
TARGET_LOOKUP = 1

brushing_extension = BrushingExtension()
brushing_radius = 200000

source_arr = np.array([source["position"] for source in sources])
source_positions = shapely.points(source_arr[:, 0], source_arr[:, 1])
source_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    pd.DataFrame.from_records(sources)[["name", "radius", "gain"]],
    geometry=source_positions,
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
# We use a lookup table (`COLORS`) to apply either the target color or the source color
# to the array
source_colors_lookup = np.where(source_gdf["gain"] > 0, TARGET_LOOKUP, SOURCE_LOOKUP)
source_fill_colors = COLORS[source_colors_lookup]

source_layer = ScatterplotLayer.from_geopandas(
    source_gdf,
    get_fill_color=source_fill_colors,
    radius_scale=3000,
    pickable=False,
    extensions=[brushing_extension],
    brushing_radius=brushing_radius,
)

targets_arr = np.array([target["position"] for target in targets])
target_positions = shapely.points(targets_arr[:, 0], targets_arr[:, 1])
target_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    pd.DataFrame.from_records(targets)[["name", "gain", "loss", "net"]],
    geometry=target_positions,
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
# We use a lookup table (`COLORS`) to apply either the target color or the source color
# to the array
target_line_colors_lookup = np.where(
    target_gdf["net"] > 0,
    TARGET_LOOKUP,
    SOURCE_LOOKUP,
)
target_line_colors = COLORS[target_line_colors_lookup]

target_ring_layer = ScatterplotLayer.from_geopandas(
    target_gdf,
    get_line_color=target_line_colors,
    radius_scale=4000,
    pickable=True,
    stroked=True,
    filled=False,
    line_width_min_pixels=2,
    extensions=[brushing_extension],
    brushing_radius=brushing_radius,
)

value = np.array([arc["value"] for arc in arcs])
get_source_position = np.array([arc["source"] for arc in arcs])
get_target_position = np.array([arc["target"] for arc in arcs])
table = pa.table({"value": value})

arc_layer = ArcLayer(
    table=table,
    get_source_position=get_source_position,
    get_target_position=get_target_position,
    get_source_color=SOURCE_COLOR,
    get_target_color=TARGET_COLOR,
    get_width=1,
    opacity=0.4,
    pickable=False,
    extensions=[brushing_extension],
    brushing_radius=brushing_radius,
)

map_ = Map([source_layer, target_ring_layer, arc_layer], picking_radius=10)
map_
GoFish style, JS (with a live brush) 
import {
  chart,
  scatter,
  circle,
  line,
  polygon,
  resolve,
  selectAll,
  filter,
  pointer,
  Color,
  Coord,
  Curve,
} from "gofish-graphics";
import { withinKm } from "@gofish/geo"; // NEW: data helper

const p = pointer(); // exists: an input; under the interaction-as-data design it is a dataset

gofish(
  container,
  { w: 960, h: 600 },
  () =>
    chart(counties, {
      coord: Coord.geo("mercator"),
      color: Color.palette({ out: SOURCE, in: TARGET }),
    })
      .mark(polygon({ points: "geometry", fill: "#f3f3f3", stroke: "#d0d0d0" }))
      .layer(
        chart(targets)
          .flow(scatter({ by: "name", at: "geometry" })) // NEW: at
          .mark(
            circle({ r: 3, fill: "none", stroke: "direction" }).name("counties")
          )
      )
      .layer(
        chart(sources)
          .flow(
            filter(withinKm("geometry", [p()], 200)),
            scatter({ at: "geometry" })
          )
          .mark(circle({ r: 2, fill: "direction" }))
      )
      .layer(
        chart(arcs)
          .flow(
            filter(withinKm(["source", "target"], [p()], 200)),
            resolve(["source", "target"], { from: selectAll("counties") })
          )
          .mark(
            line({
              from: "source",
              to: "target",
              stroke: "direction",
              opacity: 0.4,
              curve: Curve.geodesic(),
            })
          )
      ) // NEW member
);
Notes on the rewrite

Here .name("counties") is used: the arcs resolve their ends against it. The brushing extension, which in deck.gl is a GPU shader option on three layers, is an ordinary filter with the pointer as data, applied to each layer that should respond. The source-to-target color gradient on each arc is the per-segment stroke fork, below.

Fork: a color that varies along one line

deck.gl's ArcLayer blends get_source_color into get_target_color, and fastplotlib colors lines per vertex (F2). In GoFish a mark's color reads its first row (colors aggregate by "first"), so a stroke field that varies inside a line's group is silently one color.

(a) Observable Plot's rule: when the stroke varies within a series, draw the line as segments, each with its own color; no new name. Cost: the "colors read the first row" rule gets an exception for relational marks, which must be written down as a channel kind ("along").

(b) Keep the rule and make the user cut lines into segments (today's ugly version, shown in F2).

Lean (a), as a new channel kind rather than a special case.

Who owns what

The geo package still owns GoFish gives it
Geodesic arcs (Curve.geodesic), distances in km on a sphere line between named marks, the palette and its legend
Point / polygon geometry columns Layering four layers in one space, filter, the input as data
The painter, for many arcs Selection: the same brush could filter a bar chart beside the map

Gaps

  • resolve + line({ from, to }) lines are misplaced under Coord.geo. Slot: core (ref positions do not go through the coord), not the extension.
  • No color along a line (source to target). Slot: core channel kind.
  • No arc height or great-circle path. Slot: coord-aware curve (geo package).
  • No interaction in Python; the brush is frozen in both renders. Slot: interaction (the bridge does not carry signals).
  • Distance in km is hand-written (inBrush in the story). Slot: data helper in the geo package.

L4. Trips over time (lonboard air-traffic-control)

Story L4_TripsFilmstrip. SYNTHETIC tracks around JFK, three moments, each a chart in Coord.geo nested in a spread over now (the frames are data). Tracks near the window edge draw past it into the next frame, because the window does not clip.

GoFish style, Python

from gofish import chart, group, scatter, spread, line, filter, between, field, Coord
from gofish_geo import read_parquet  # NEW: source

traces = read_parquet(url)
frames = traces.with_columns(now=...)  # a filmstrip: one copy of the rows per moment
(
    chart(frames)
    .flow(spread(by="now", dir="x"))
    .mark(
        chart(coord=Coord.geo("mercator"))
        .flow(
            filter(between(field("timestamp"), field("now") - 200, field("now"))),
            group(by="flight"),
            scatter(by="timestamp", at="geometry"),
        )
        .mark(line(stroke="rgb(30,30,200)", stroke_width=2, opacity=0.8))
    )
)
The lonboard program

Source: https://github.com/developmentseed/lonboard/blob/main/examples/air-traffic-control.ipynb 

from datetime import timedelta
from io import BytesIO

import requests
from arro3.io import read_parquet

from lonboard import Map, TripsLayer

# Fetch the Parquet file and parse to an Arrow table
url = "https://github.com/kylebarron/adsb-extract/releases/download/v0.1/2024-10-03_traces.parquet"
r = requests.get(url)
table = read_parquet(BytesIO(r.content)).read_all()

layer = TripsLayer(
    table=table,
    get_timestamps=table["timestamp"],
    width_min_pixels=2,
    get_color=[30, 30, 200, 200],
    trail_length=200,
    # Turn off tooltip data selection for better performance
    pickable=False,
)

m = Map(
    layer,
    view_state={
        "longitude": -73.8,
        "latitude": 40.6,
        "zoom": 9.5,
        "pitch": 50.6,
        "bearing": 8.24,
    },
    # Increase height of generated map
    height=800,
)
m

layer.animate(step=timedelta(minutes=1), fps=50)

layer.stop_animation()
GoFish style, JS

A trip is a line through the rows of one flight in time order, and the trail is a window on time. The clock is an input, and the window is a filter with between, which exists. The animation is GoFish's own time.sequence, which is JS-only today. 

import {
  chart,
  group,
  scatter,
  line,
  filter,
  between,
  field,
  time,
  Coord,
} from "gofish-graphics";
import { basemap, readParquet, Painter } from "@gofish/geo"; // NEW: basemap, readParquet, Painter

const traces = await readParquet(url); // one row per position: flight, timestamp, geometry
const TRAIL = 200; // seconds, as trail_length

chart(traces, {
  coord: Coord.geo("mercator", { lon: [-74.4, -73.2], lat: [40.3, 40.9] }),
})
  .mark(basemap("carto-positron")) // NEW
  .layer(
    chart(traces)
      .flow(
        time.sequence({ by: "now", every: 60 }), // NEW option `every` (see note)
        filter(
          between(field("timestamp"), field("now").minus(TRAIL), field("now"))
        ), // NEW: .minus
        group({ by: "flight" }),
        scatter({ by: "timestamp", at: "geometry" }) // NEW: at
      )
      .mark(line({ stroke: "rgb(30,30,200)", strokeWidth: 2, opacity: 0.8 }))
  )
  .render(container, { h: 800, painter: Painter.deckgl() });
Notes on the rewrite

The honest part: time.sequence({ by }) plays the groups of an existing column. A clock that steps through a continuous timestamp every 60 s, and a window that reads the current step, do not have a spelling yet; every and .minus above are placeholders for that missing piece, and the clean answer probably comes from the animation-grammar work (time as an axis), not from the geo package. Lonboard's pitch and bearing (a 3D camera) have no GoFish counterpart at all.

Python has no clock, so the Python program draws the moments side by side, which is what the render below does in JS.

Who owns what

The geo package still owns GoFish gives it
Reading ADS-B traces (Arrow), point geometry group + scatter + line for a path, filter/between for the trail
The basemap, the 3D camera (pitch, bearing) The clock and the filmstrip (time as data), composition with a time chart
The painter for 1e5 trails Legend, selection of one flight with selectAll

Gaps

  • No stepping clock over a continuous time column, and no way to read the current time inside a window filter. Slot: core (time), not the extension.
  • No clipping to the coord window. Slot: core.
  • No 3D camera. Slot: painter (deck.gl), and a GoFish view model that does not exist.
  • No basemap. Slot: source and mark.

fastplotlib

F1. Image and colormap (fastplotlib image_cmap)

Story F1_ImageCmap. A SYNTHETIC 48 x 48 image (Gaussian blobs), as 2,304 rects, under viridis and under the custom orange-purple-green stops. The colorbars come for free. The two panels are two renders: in one render, sibling charts share the first chart's color scale (see walls).

GoFish style, Python

import imageio.v3 as iio
from gofish import chart, scatter, rect, datum, Color
from gofish_fpl import (
    array,
    Painter,
)  # NEW: array (source), Painter.pygfx (family member)

im = array(iio.imread("imageio:camera.png"), dims=("y", "x"), name="v")  # NEW


def view(cmap):
    return (
        chart(im, color=Color.gradient(cmap))
        .flow(scatter(x="x", y="y"))
        .mark(rect(w=datum(1), h=datum(1), fill="v"))
    )


view("viridis").render(w=700, h=560, painter=Painter.pygfx())  # NEW
view(["orange", "purple", "green"]).render(w=700, h=560, painter=Painter.pygfx())
The fastplotlib program

Source: https://github.com/fastplotlib/fastplotlib/blob/main/examples/image/image_cmap.py 

"""
Image Colormap
==============

Example showing simple plot creation and subsequent cmap change with a standard image from imageio.
"""

figure.show()
