GoFish style, JS 
import { chart, scatter, rect, datum, Color } from "gofish-graphics";
import { array } from "@gofish/fpl"; // NEW: source

const im = array(pixels, { dims: ["y", "x"], name: "v", shape: [512, 512] }); // NEW

const view = (cmap) =>
  chart(im, { color: Color.gradient(cmap) })
    .flow(scatter({ x: "x", y: "y" }))
    .mark(rect({ w: datum(1), h: datum(1), fill: "v" }));

view("viridis").render(container, { w: 700, h: 560 });
Notes on the rewrite

fastplotlib changes the colormap of a live graphic (image.cmap = ...). GoFish rebuilds the spec with a new color scale; with the reactive layer the cmap could be a signal, and only paint changes.

Fork: how an array becomes chart data

(a) An array source, array(data, { dims }), that is a table with one row per element and one column per dim plus the value: (y, x, v). The image is then a grid of data-unit rects, an ordinary mark, so anything else in the same data space (ROI contours in F4, circles in F3) lines up with it, and the color scale, colorbar and selection are the usual ones. The painter sees a regular grid of unit rects with one fill channel and draws one texture: that is a reduction at drawing time, in line with the decision that selectAll is a logical selection over the marks the spec defines, not the drawn ones. The dim names come from xarray (dims), which scientists already use.

(b) A dedicated raster mark that takes a 2D array per row (raster({ values })). Cost: a second way to draw a grid, which does not compose with partition, table or the 2D histogram in P1, and a second color path.

Lean (a). The cost of (a) is the verbose mark, rect({ w: datum(1), h: datum(1) }); a table({ by: { x, y }, spacing: 0 }) spelling is shorter but puts the image in band space, where a continuous overlay cannot follow.

Who owns what

The fpl package still owns GoFish gives it
The array source (numpy, xarray, zarr, lazy slices) Color scales, colorbar, axes in pixel units
The pygfx painter (texture for a rect grid, GPU colormap) Overlays in the same data space, composition, selection

Gaps

  • 512 x 512 = 262,144 rects is past what the SVG painter can draw. Slot: painter (a texture reduction).
  • Thin seams between cells (anti-aliasing); a texture painter would not have them. The story strokes each cell in its own color to hide them. Slot: painter.
  • Sibling charts in one render share one color scale. Slot: core.
  • No array source; the story builds rows by hand. Slot: source.

F2. Line stack (fastplotlib line_stack)

Story F2_LineStack, three renders. Panels 1 and 2 are the ugly version that works today: each line cut into 99 two-point segments in a derive, then group({ by: "seg" }), so each segment takes one color. Panel 3 is direct. The stack offset is spacing: -8 px (a negative box spacing that overlaps the bands), not a pitch in y units.

GoFish style, Python

import numpy as np
from gofish import chart, spread, scatter, line, Color, Spacing
from gofish_fpl import array  # NEW: source

lines = array(multi_data, dims=("line", "i", "xy"), name="v").pivot(
    "xy", ["x", "y"]
)  # NEW: .pivot


def stack(**stroke):
    return chart(lines, **stroke).flow(
        spread(by="line", dir="y", spacing=Spacing.pitch(1)),  # separation, in y units
        scatter(by="i", x="x", y="y"),
    )


stack(color=Color.gradient("jet")).mark(line(stroke="i"))  # jet along each line
stack(color=Color.gradient("bwr")).mark(line(stroke="y"))  # bwr along each line, by y
stack(color=Color.gradient("viridis")).mark(line(stroke="line"))  # viridis across lines
The fastplotlib program

Source: https://github.com/fastplotlib/fastplotlib/blob/main/examples/line_collection/line_stack.py 

"""
Line Stack
==========

Example showing how to plot a stack of lines
"""

# test_example = true
# sphinx_gallery_pygfx_docs = 'screenshot'

import numpy as np
import fastplotlib as fpl
import cmap as cmap_lib
from itertools import repeat

xs = np.linspace(0, np.pi * 10, 100)
# sine wave
ys = np.sin(xs)

data = np.column_stack([xs, ys])
multi_data = np.stack([data] * 10)

figure = fpl.Figure(
    shape=(3, 1),
    size=(700, 1200),
)

# colormap per-line
line_stack = figure[0, 0].add_line_stack(
    multi_data,  # shape: (10, 100, 2), i.e. [n_lines, n_points, xy]
    cmap=["jet"] * 10,
    separation=(0, 0, 0),  # spacing between lines along each axis (x, y, z)
    separation_axis="y",
)

# colormap per-line with per-line transform
line_stack2 = figure[1, 0].add_line_stack(
    multi_data,  # shape: (10, 100, 2), i.e. [n_lines, n_points, xy]
    cmap=["bwr"] * 10,
    cmap_transform=np.broadcast_to(ys, (10, ys.size)),
    separation=(0, 0, 0),  # spacing between lines along each axis (x, y, z)
    separation_axis="y",
)

# colormap across-lines
line_stack3 = figure[2, 0].add_line_stack(
    multi_data,  # shape: (10, 100, 2), i.e. [n_lines, n_points, xy]
    cmap="viridis",
    separation=(0, 0, 0),  # spacing between lines along each axis (x, y, z)
    separation_axis="y",
)


figure.show(maintain_aspect=False)


# NOTE: fpl.loop.run() should not be used for interactive sessions
# See the "JupyterLab and IPython" section in the user guide
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(__doc__)
    fpl.loop.run()

(The example passes separation=(0, 0, 0); the render below uses a nonzero separation so the stack is visible.)

GoFish style, JS 
const lines = array(multiData, { dims: ["line", "i", "xy"], name: "v" }).pivot(
  "xy",
  ["x", "y"]
); // NEW
const stack = (opts) =>
  chart(lines, opts).flow(
    spread({ by: "line", dir: "y", spacing: Spacing.pitch(1) }),
    scatter({ by: "i", x: "x", y: "y" })
  );
stack({ color: Color.gradient("jet") }).mark(line({ stroke: "i" }));
stack({ color: Color.gradient("bwr") }).mark(line({ stroke: "y" }));
stack({ color: Color.gradient("viridis") }).mark(line({ stroke: "line" }));
Notes on the rewrite

fastplotlib's separation is a distance between the same point on each line, which is exactly Spacing.pitch(distance) (GoFish's word for a fixed distance between repeated items). The trailing xy axis of an (n, 100, 2) array is a pair of columns, not a dim; .pivot (polars' name) turns it into x and y, or scatter({ at: "v" }) reads the pair as a point (the same at option as L1). The first two panels need the per-segment stroke from the L3 fork: line({ stroke: "i" }) where i varies inside each line.

Who owns what

The fpl package still owns GoFish gives it
The (lines, points, xy) array as rows spread for the stack, scatter + line, colorbar
The pygfx painter for 1e3 lines x 1e4 points Axes with the line index as labels, selection of a line

Gaps

  • No color along a line; segments by hand. Slot: core channel kind.
  • Spacing.pitch is in pixels; a separation in data units has no spelling. Slot: core.
  • No array source or .pivot. Slot: source.

F3. Grid figure (fastplotlib multigraphic_gridplot)

Story F3_Grid, four renders in a CSS grid (one render each, because of the shared color scale), SYNTHETIC images in place of coffee.png and coins.png. Overlays are .layer() on the image chart and line up with it. Two workarounds are visible: the tab10 circle colors are looked up by hand (with stroke: "label" the circles drew nothing, because the render's one color scale is the image's gradient), and the overlay is blue rects, not an RGBA image. A first try with layer([imageChart, overlayChart]) instead of .layer() put the overlay in its own space, with its own axes, offset from the image.

GoFish style, Python

from gofish import (
    chart,
    spread,
    scatter,
    filter,
    field,
    rect,
    circle,
    line,
    datum,
    Color,
    Spacing,
)
from gofish_fpl import array  # NEW: source

img = array(coffee_gray, dims=("y", "x"), name="v")  # NEW
coins = array(img2, dims=("y", "x"), name="v")


def image(a, cmap):
    return (
        chart(a, color=Color.gradient(cmap))
        .flow(scatter(x="x", y="y"))
        .mark(rect(w=datum(1), h=datum(1), fill="v"))
    )


image_overlay = image(img, "viridis").layer(
    chart(img)
    .flow(filter(field("v") > 200), scatter(x="x", y="y"))
    .mark(rect(w=datum(1), h=datum(1), fill="blue", opacity=0.6))
)
circles = image(coins, "gray").layer(
    chart(centers, color=Color.palette("tableau10"))  # one row per circle, label column
    .flow(scatter(x="cx", y="cy"))
    .mark(circle(r=datum(5), fill="none", stroke="label", stroke_width=3, opacity=0.5))
)
line_stack = (
    chart(sines, color=Color.gradient("Wistia"))
    .flow(
        spread(by="line", dir="y", spacing=Spacing.pitch(1)),
        scatter(by="i", x="x", y="y"),
    )
    .mark(line(stroke="line"))
)
clouds = (
    chart(cloud_a, color=Color.gradient("jet"))
    .flow(scatter(x="x", y="y"))
    .mark(circle(r=2, fill="i"))
    .layer(chart(cloud_b).flow(scatter(x="x", y="y")).mark(circle(r=2, fill="red")))
)

spread(
    [spread([image_overlay, circles], dir="x"), spread([line_stack, clouds], dir="x")],
    dir="y",
).render(w=700, h=560)
The fastplotlib program

Source: https://github.com/fastplotlib/fastplotlib/blob/main/examples/gridplot/multigraphic_gridplot.py 

"""
Multi-Graphic Grid layout
=========================

A Figure with multiple subplots and multiple graphic types.
"""

# test_example = false
# sphinx_gallery_pygfx_docs = 'screenshot'

import fastplotlib as fpl
import numpy as np
import imageio.v3 as iio
from itertools import product

# define figure
figure = fpl.Figure(
    shape=(2, 2),
    names=[["image-overlay", "circles"], ["line-stack", "scatter"]],
    size=(700, 560),
)

img = iio.imread("imageio:coffee.png")

# add image to subplot
figure["image-overlay"].add_image(data=img)

# generate overlay

# empty array for overlay, shape is [nrows, ncols, RGBA]
overlay = np.zeros(shape=(*img.shape[:2], 4), dtype=np.float32)

# set the blue values of some pixels with an alpha > 1
overlay[img[:, :, -1] > 200] = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.6]).astype(np.float32)

# add overlay to image
figure["image-overlay"].add_image(data=overlay)


# generate some circles
def make_circle(center, radius: float, n_points: int = 75) -> np.ndarray:
    theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n_points)
    xs = radius * np.sin(theta)
    ys = radius * np.cos(theta)

    return np.column_stack([xs, ys]) + center


spatial_dims = (50, 50)

# this makes 16 circles, so we can create 16 cmap values, so it will use these values to set the
# color of the line based by using the cmap as a LUT with the corresponding cmap_transform
circles = list()
for center in product(range(0, spatial_dims[0], 15), range(0, spatial_dims[1], 15)):
    circles.append(make_circle(center, 5, n_points=75))

# things like class labels, cluster labels, etc.
cmap_transform = [
    [0, 1, 1, 2],
    [0, 0, 1, 1],
    [2, 2, 8, 3],
    [1, 9, 1, 5],
]

# add an image to overlay the circles on
img2 = iio.imread("imageio:coins.png")[10::5, 5::5]

figure["circles"].add_image(data=img2, cmap="gray")

# add the circles to the figure
figure["circles"].add_line_collection(
    circles,
    cmap="tab10",
    cmap_transform=np.asarray(cmap_transform).ravel(),
    thickness=3,
    alpha=0.5,
    name="circles-graphic",
)

# move the circles graphic so that it is centered over the image
figure["circles"]["circles-graphic"].offset = np.array([7, 7, 2])

# generate some sine data
# linspace, create 100 evenly spaced x values from -10 to 10
xs = np.linspace(-10, 10, 100)
# sine wave
ys = np.sin(xs)
sine = np.column_stack([xs, ys])

# make 10 identical waves
sine_waves = 15 * [sine]

# add the line stack to the figure
figure["line-stack"].add_line_stack(
    data=sine_waves, cmap="Wistia", separation=(0, 1, 0)
)

figure["line-stack"].auto_scale(maintain_aspect=False)

# generate some scatter data
# create a gaussian cloud of 500 points
n_points = 500

mean = [0, 0]  # mean of the Gaussian distribution
covariance = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]  # covariance matrix

gaussian_cloud = np.random.multivariate_normal(mean, covariance, n_points)
gaussian_cloud2 = np.random.multivariate_normal(mean, covariance, n_points)

# add the scatter graphics to the figure
figure["scatter"].add_scatter(data=gaussian_cloud, sizes=2, cmap="jet")
figure["scatter"].add_scatter(data=gaussian_cloud2, colors="r", sizes=2)

figure.show()

# NOTE: fpl.loop.run() should not be used for interactive sessions
# See the "JupyterLab and IPython" section in the user guide
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(__doc__)
    fpl.loop.run()
Notes on the rewrite

The JS program is the same with object options. The grid is two nested spreads (or table), which already exist. What fastplotlib does with graphic.offset = [7, 7, 2] (move the circles to sit on the image) is not needed: the circles are in the image's data space because they are a .layer() of the image chart. The overlay that fastplotlib builds as a second RGBA image is a filter plus a second rect layer. Wistia is not a built-in scheme; it would be a list of stops.

Who owns what

The fpl package still owns GoFish gives it
Arrays and RGBA images as data The grid (spread / table), overlays in one data space
The painter (textures, 1e6 points) Legends per panel, axes, selection across panels

Gaps

  • One color scale per render: two colormaps, or a gradient plus a palette, cannot share a render. Slot: core. This is the most common wall in the corpus.
  • layer([a, b]) of two charts does not share a data space; .layer() on the builder does. Two spellings with different spaces is a trap. Slot: core.
  • RGB(A) images have no color-channel story: a pixel's color is the data. Slot: data type (an RGB value type that the fill reads raw).

F4. Movie with a time slider and a selector driving other plots (fastplotlib ImageWidget and LinearRegionSelector)

Story F4_MovieTracesSlider. The slider works and drives both the frame and the time markers on the traces. The data is SYNTHETIC: a 40 by 40, 60-frame movie with five ROIs, and the frame is a grid of rects, not a texture. Three workarounds and one fault are visible:

  • The ROI colors are looked up by hand from a tab10 list, because the render's one color scale is the frame's gray gradient.
  • The trace offsets are computed by hand (y = f + 1.3 * roi). With spread({ by: "roi" }) in both the traces and the marker layer, the two spreads did not line up, and the panel overflowed its box.
  • A first version drew the current time as a fixed 220 px rect in the traces layer. A fixed pixel size in a layered visualization pushed the layout to 440 px tall, so the markers are dots instead.
  • Fault, not fixed: the traces panel's y axis runs 0 to 40, the image's range. The sibling charts under one spread share the y domain as well as the color scale, so the traces are squashed into the bottom eighth.

GoFish style, Python

from gofish import (
    chart,
    spread,
    scatter,
    group,
    filter,
    between,
    field,
    rect,
    circle,
    line,
    datum,
    Color,
)
from gofish import slider  # NEW (Python): input as dataset
from gofish_fpl import array  # NEW: source

movie = array(frames, dims=("t", "y", "x"), name="v")  # NEW: one row per element
t = slider(domain=(0, 59), step=1, value=23)  # NEW (Python): a one-row dataset

frame = (
    chart(movie, color=Color.gradient("gray"))
    .flow(
        filter(field("t") == t.value),  # window: between(t.value - 2, t.value + 2)
        group(by=("x", "y")),
        scatter(x="x", y="y"),
    )
    .mark(rect(w=datum(1), h=datum(1), fill=field("v").mean()))
    .layer(
        chart(rois, color=Color.palette("tableau10"))
        .flow(scatter(x="cx", y="cy"))
        .mark(circle(r=datum(3), fill="none", stroke="roi", stroke_width=2))
    )
)

traces_view = (
    chart(traces, color=Color.palette("tableau10"))
    .flow(spread(by="roi", dir="y"), scatter(by="t", x="t", y="f"))
    .mark(line(stroke="roi"))
    .layer(
        chart(traces)
        .flow(
            filter(field("t") == t.value),
            spread(by="roi", dir="y"),
            scatter(x="t", y="f"),
        )
        .mark(circle(r=4, fill="#f0b400"))
    )
)

spread(spread(frame, traces_view, dir="x"), t, dir="y").render(w=820, h=300)
The fastplotlib program

Source: https://github.com/fastplotlib/fastplotlib/blob/main/examples/image_widget/image_widget_single_video.py, with the selector from https://github.com/fastplotlib/fastplotlib/blob/main/examples/selection_tools/linear_region_line_collection.py. 

"""
Image widget Video
==================

Example showing how to scroll through one or more videos using the ImageWidget
"""

# test_example = true
# sphinx_gallery_pygfx_docs = 'animate 6s 20fps'

import fastplotlib as fpl
import imageio.v3 as iio
import numpy as np

movie = iio.imread("imageio:cockatoo.mp4")

# Ignore and do not use the next 2 lines
# for the purposes of docs gallery generation we subsample and only use 15 frames
movie_sub = movie[:15, ::12, ::12].copy()
del movie

iw = fpl.ImageWidget(movie_sub, rgb=True, figure_kwargs={"size": (700, 560)})

# ImageWidget supports setting window functions the `time` "t" or `volume` "z" dimension
# These can also be given as kwargs to `ImageWidget` during instantiation
# to set a window function, give a dict in the form of {dim: (func, window_size)}
iw.window_funcs = {"t": (np.mean, 5)}

# change the window size
iw.window_funcs = {"t": (np.mean, 2)}

# change the function
iw.window_funcs = {"t": (np.max, 2)}

# or reset it
iw.window_funcs = None

iw.show()

figure = iw.figure

# NOTE: fpl.loop.run() should not be used for interactive sessions
# See the "JupyterLab and IPython" section in the user guide
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(__doc__)
    fpl.loop.run()

The combined program this example stands for is the common neuroscience view: a calcium-imaging movie with a time slider, regions of interest (ROIs) drawn on the frame, one fluorescence trace per ROI beside it, and a marker on each trace at the current time.

GoFish style, JS 
import {
  chart,
  spread,
  scatter,
  group,
  filter,
  field,
  rect,
  circle,
  line,
  datum,
  Color,
  signal,
  slider,
  gofish,
} from "gofish-graphics";
import { array } from "@gofish/fpl"; // NEW: source

const movie = array(frames, { dims: ["t", "y", "x"], name: "v" }); // NEW
const t = signal(23);

gofish(container, { w: 820, h: 300 }, () =>
  spread({ dir: "y" }, [
    spread({ dir: "x" }, [
      chart(movie, { color: Color.gradient("gray") })
        .flow(filter(field("t").eq(t())), scatter({ x: "x", y: "y" }))
        .mark(rect({ w: datum(1), h: datum(1), fill: "v" }))
        .layer(
          chart(rois, { color: Color.palette("tableau10") })
            .flow(scatter({ x: "cx", y: "cy" }))
            .mark(circle({ r: datum(3), fill: "none", stroke: "roi" }))
        ),
      chart(traces, { color: Color.palette("tableau10") })
        .flow(
          spread({ by: "roi", dir: "y" }),
          scatter({ by: "t", x: "t", y: "f" })
        )
        .mark(line({ stroke: "roi" }))
        .layer(
          chart(traces)
            .flow(
              filter(field("t").eq(t())),
              spread({ by: "roi", dir: "y" }),
              scatter({ x: "t", y: "f" })
            )
            .mark(circle({ r: 4, fill: "#f0b400" }))
        ),
    ]),
    slider({ value: t, onInput: (v) => t.set(v), domain: [0, 59], step: 1 }),
  ])
);
Notes on the rewrite

The window function (window_funcs = {"t": (np.mean, 5)}) is not a new option: it is filter(between(t - 2, t + 2)), then group by pixel, then .mean() on the fill. The LinearRegionSelector from the second source is the same pattern: the selection is a two-row dataset (or a signal pair) that other views read in a filter. No bind or when is needed.

The image is a grid of data-unit rects, an ordinary mark, so the region circles line up with it because they are a .layer() in the same data space. fastplotlib needs graphic.offset for that. The window function is filter(between(...)) plus group plus .mean(), not a new option. A pygfx painter would draw the rect grid as one texture.

Who owns what

The fpl package still owns GoFish gives it
Reading movies and ndarrays with named dims The slider as an input, and filters that read it
The painter: a texture per frame, frame rate Window functions as filter + group + .mean()
Video decoding and caching frames Linked views: frame, ROIs, traces and markers in one spec

Gaps

  • Sibling charts in one spread share scales: color for sure, and here the y domain too. Slot: core. Same wall as F1, F2, F3 and P1.
  • Two spread({ by }) in a chart and its .layer() do not line up. Slot: core.
  • A fixed pixel size inside a layer breaks the layout. Slot: core.
  • Python has no inputs or reactivity: slider and signals exist only in JS. Slot: Python bridge.
  • A whole movie as rect rows is far too slow in SVG (40x40x60 = 96 000 rows here; a real movie has 1e8). Needs the painter slot and a source that only materializes the filtered frame. Slot: painter, source.

progressive

P1. Progressive 2D histogram (ProgressiVis, NYC taxi)

Story P1_ProgressiveHeatmap: the same spec at 1%, 10%, 50% and 100% of 20 000 SYNTHETIC pickups, one render each, with Bin.step(0.01) (about 60 by 40 cells) since SVG cannot draw 512 by 512 cells quickly. The caption is HTML, not GoFish. Two faults are visible, and both are the stability questions a progressive system has to answer:

  • The color domain changes every frame (max count 7, 43, 214, 419), so a cell's color does not mean the same thing from one frame to the next. Domain.continuous would fix it, but it is announced in the docs and not built.
  • The cells cover only the extent of the data seen so far, not the coord's window. At 1% the grid is smaller and sits in a different place than at 100%. The bins should start from the window, as Histogram2D does with its min and max inputs.

GoFish style, Python

from gofish import (
    chart,
    partition,
    region,
    field,
    text,
    Bin,
    Coord,
    Color,
    Domain,
)  # Domain.continuous: PLANNED
from gofish_progressive import csv  # NEW: source

taxi = csv(LARGE_TAXI_FILE, columns=["pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude"])  # NEW

chart(
    taxi,
    coord=Coord.geo("mercator", lon=(-74.27, -73.68), lat=(40.49, 40.92)),
    color=Color.gradient("viridis", domain=Domain.continuous(0, 400)),
).flow(
    partition(
        by={
            "x": field("pickup_longitude").bin(Bin.thresholds(512)),
            "y": field("pickup_latitude").bin(Bin.thresholds(512)),
        }
    )
).mark(
    region(fill=field("pickup_longitude").count())
).layer(
    chart(taxi.progress).mark(text(text="fraction"))
)  # NEW: a one-row dataset
The ProgressiVis program

Source: https://progressivis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/userguide2.html 

from progressivis import CSVLoader, Histogram2D, ConstDict, Heatmap, PDict
from dataclasses import dataclass

LARGE_TAXI_FILE = "https://www.aviz.fr/nyc-taxi/yellow_tripdata_2015-01.csv.bz2"
RESOLUTION = 512


@dataclass
class Bounds:
    top: float = 40.92
    bottom: float = 40.49
    left: float = -74.27
    right: float = -73.68


bounds = Bounds()
col_x = "pickup_longitude"
col_y = "pickup_latitude"


csv = CSVLoader(LARGE_TAXI_FILE, index_col=False, usecols=[col_x, col_y])

min = ConstDict(PDict({col_x: bounds.left, col_y: bounds.bottom}))
max = ConstDict(PDict({col_x: bounds.right, col_y: bounds.top}))

histogram2d = Histogram2D(col_x, col_y, xbins=RESOLUTION, ybins=RESOLUTION)
histogram2d.input.table = csv.output.result
histogram2d.input.min = min.output.result
histogram2d.input.max = max.output.result

heatmap = Heatmap()
heatmap.input.array = histogram2d.output.result
...

ProgressiVis is a dataflow of modules. Each module runs on the next chunk of rows and pushes a partial result downstream, so the heatmap fills in while the 2 GB file is still loading.

GoFish style, JS 
import {
  chart,
  partition,
  region,
  field,
  text,
  Bin,
  Coord,
  Color,
  Domain,
} from "gofish-graphics"; // Domain: PLANNED
import { csv } from "@gofish/progressive"; // NEW: source

const taxi = csv(LARGE_TAXI_FILE, {
  columns: ["pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude"],
}); // NEW

chart(taxi, {
  coord: Coord.geo("mercator", { lon: [-74.27, -73.68], lat: [40.49, 40.92] }),
  color: Color.gradient("viridis", { domain: Domain.continuous(0, 400) }),
})
  .flow(
    partition({
      by: {
        x: field("pickup_longitude").bin(Bin.thresholds(512)),
        y: field("pickup_latitude").bin(Bin.thresholds(512)),
      },
    })
  )
  .mark(region({ fill: field("pickup_longitude").count() }))
  .layer(chart(taxi.progress).mark(text({ text: "fraction" }))) // NEW
  .render(container, { w: 400, h: 400 });
Notes on the rewrite

The spec is the same as for an array of rows. Only the data argument differs. The notebook's ConstDict bounds are the coord's lon and lat window, and Histogram2D is partition with binned fields and a count fill. The progress readout is a dataset the source exposes, drawn like any other data.

Who owns what

The progressive package owns GoFish gives it
Chunked reading, the scheduler, partial aggregates The binning and the count as a spec it can plan from
Incremental re-run on each chunk Color legend, map window, layering with other data
The progress dataset A progress readout drawn as ordinary data

Gaps

  • No declared continuous domain for a color scale. Slot: core (planned as Domain.continuous).
  • Bins follow the data's extent, not the window. Slot: core.
  • No progressive source, no progress dataset, no incremental re-run: today the whole spec runs again on all rows. Slot: source, and a core hook that lets an aggregate be updated by a chunk.
  • 512 by 512 cells needs the painter slot (an image, measured at 1e7 cells in 380 ms). Slot: painter.

What the corpus says overall

Count
Programs rewritten and rendered 9 (4 lonboard, 4 fastplotlib, 1 progressive)
Names that do not exist today 16
Of those, in a domain package 9: basemap, readParquet, H3, EPSG codes in Coord.geo, withinKm, Curve.geodesic(), array and .pivot, csv, source.progress
Of those, in core 7: scatter({ at }), the Painter family and .render({ painter }), Domain.continuous (announced, not built), field().minus, time.sequence({ every }), slider in Python, color that varies along a line

Two findings matter more than the count.

The spec does not change with the painter or the source. In all nine rewrites the marks are the ones GoFish has. The domain package adds a column type, a source, a strategy member, or a painter. A progressive source differs from a static one only in the data argument.

The worst walls are in core, not in the extension slots. The most common wall is that one render has one set of scales: sibling panels share the first panel's color scale, and in the movie example the traces panel also took the image's y range, so the traces are squashed. Five of nine examples hit it. An extension architecture does not fix this; it has to be fixed for "fastplotlib programs in GoFish style" to be true. The full list of fifteen walls is at the end of examples.md.

The forks, in one place

These spellings had a real fork. Each is argued where it bites; this is the index.

Fork Where it bites Lean
Where the painter is chosen L1 A .render(painter=Painter.deckgl()) option, default SVG. The spec does not change.
How a basemap enters L1, L3 A mark in the layer (basemap("carto-positron")), first in paint order. Not a coord property.
How a projection or CRS is spelled L1, L2 Keep Coord.geo(projection, { lon, lat }). The geo package widens what projection accepts (an EPSG code) and the geometry type carries the data's CRS. No new coord name.
How a point-valued column is placed L1, L3, F2 scatter({ at: "geometry" }), one new option, also for fastplotlib's (n, 2) arrays. The other spelling is two field methods.
How a color varies along one line L3, F2 A stroke that varies within a line's group draws per segment (Observable Plot's rule). Today it is an error-free silent first-row read.
How an array becomes rows F1, F4 array(movie, { dims: ["t", "y", "x"] }) is a table with one row per element. An image is a grid of data-unit rects; the painter, not a new mark, turns it into a texture.
How an input enters L3, F4 The input is a dataset or a signal read in filter; no bind or when. A window function is filter(between(...)) plus group plus .mean().
How a progressive source differs P1 Only in the data argument. Marks are the same; stability comes from fixed bins and a declared domain.

Invented names

Every name below is marked NEW in the code above. A domain package means one of the extension packages the proposal sketches (gofish_geo, gofish_fpl, gofish_progressive); core means gofish-graphics itself.

Name Kind Where Examples Nearest existing spelling
basemap(style) mark geo package L1, L4 none; polygon over a hand-loaded ring table (what the stories do)
scatter({ at }) option core L1, L3, L4 scatter({ x: "lon", y: "lat" }) on exploded columns
Painter with .svg(), .deckgl(), .pygfx() strategy family, render option painter core family, members from packages L1, F1 none; the renderer is fixed to SVG
readParquet / read_parquet source (GeoArrow table) geo package L1, L4 a JS array of rows
H3 data type (a hexagon cell id) geo package L2 polygon({ points }) on precomputed rings
EPSG codes in Coord.geo new accepted value, not a new name geo package L1, L2 Coord.geo("mercator"), a d3 projection name
withinKm / within_km data helper (distance predicate) geo package L3 a hand-written filter with a haversine function
Curve.geodesic() family member geo package L3 Curve.arc, Curve.perfectArrows
field(...).minus(...) field method core L4 a precomputed column in derive
time.sequence({ every }) option core L4 time.sequence({ by }) (JS only)
array(nd, { dims, name }) and .pivot source fpl package F1, F2, F3, F4 an array of { x, y, v } rows built by hand
slider in Python input as a dataset Python bridge F4 JS signal + slider
csv(url, { columns }) progressive source progressive package P1 an array of rows
source.progress one-row dataset progressive package P1 none; an HTML caption in the story
Domain.continuous(lo, hi) family member, PLANNED core L1, L2, P1 Domain.discrete(levels)
A stroke that varies within a line draws per segment rule change, no new name core L3, F2 today the line reads its first row; the stories split lines into two-point segments by hand

Nine of the sixteen live in a domain package, and one in the Python bridge. The core additions are scatter({ at }), the Painter slot, field().minus, the every option, and the planned Domain.continuous; the along-line color rule changes meaning but adds no name.

Walls, most serious first

Each wall is something the stories hit today with public names only. None was patched in library source; the workaround each story uses is declared in its comments and in its section above.

  1. One set of scales per render. Sibling charts under one combinator share the first chart's color scale (F1, F2, F3, P1) and, in F4, the y domain too. A categorical stroke under a render whose color scale is a gradient draws nothing (F3, F4). Workaround: one render per panel in a CSS grid, and hand lookups into a tab10 list. This bites every example with more than one panel, so it comes first.
  2. No painter slot. Every render is SVG. One million points takes 9.3 s in SVG, against 35 ms in WebGL; a 512 by 512 heatmap or a real movie cannot be drawn as rects, and a rect-grid image shows seams (F1, F3, F4). The stories use small SYNTHETIC data to stay under the 30 s capture limit.
  3. Data-unit lengths under Coord.geo are wrong and slow. A circle radius given in data units (meters in lonboard) draws as a stretched box and timed out (L1). Workaround: a fixed pixel radius.
  4. layer([chartA, chartB]) does not share a data space, while chartA.layer(chartB) does (L3, F3). Two spellings that look the same give different positions. Workaround: always use the builder method.
  5. resolve + line({ from, to }) is misplaced under Coord.geo (L3, evidence in img/ex-L3-wall-ref-lines.png). Workaround: endpoint rows, group by arc, scatter the two ends, draw a line.
  6. No color that varies along one line, neither per vertex (F2) nor source to target (L3). Workaround: split each line into two-point segments by hand.
  7. No map tiles and no clipping to the geo window. There is no basemap source or mark, and polygons outside the window spill past it; the legend can overlap the map (L1, L3).
  8. No declared continuous domain, and bins follow the data's extent. Colors change meaning between frames of a progressive render, and the cell grid moves (P1); a clamp for outliers is a hand derive (L1, L2). Domain.continuous is announced but not built.
  9. No geometry, H3 or CRS types. Lon and lat must be exploded into columns, and hexagons into polygon rings, before GoFish sees them (L1, L2, L3).
  10. Python has no reactivity. signal, slider and time are JS only, so the F4 and L4 interactions have no Python spelling today.
  11. No progressive source, no progress readout, no incremental re-run (P1).
  12. A fixed pixel size inside a layer breaks the layout. A 220 px time cursor in a 220 px chart made the layout 440 px tall (F4). Workaround: dots at the current time.
  13. Two spread({ by }) in a chart and its .layer() do not line up (F4). Workaround: the stack offset computed by hand.
  14. A data-sized image needs datum(1) on both w and h, which is verbose for the most common array view (F1 to F4).
  15. Curve.arc draws semicircles that are too big for flow arcs on a map (L3). Minor.

Terms

  • Engine. The part of GoFish that turns a spec into a display list: build, resolve, the scale and layout solve, and lowering. It is the "middle".
  • Display list. The picture as plain data: a list of rects, ellipses, paths, text, images, groups and composites in pixels. It exists today (toDisplayList) and is the only render path.
  • Painter. Code that draws a display list. Today there is one in use, the SolidJS SVG painter.
  • Host. The program the engine runs in. It answers the questions the engine cannot answer alone: how wide is this text, how big is this image, what does this Python callback return. Today the only real host is a browser.
  • Source. The data argument of chart(...). Today it is always rows in memory.
  • Extension package. A package that adds constructs to GoFish: a data type, a source, a coord, a mark, a strategy, or a painter.

What is already true in the code

The survey of the engine found that much of step 1 exists.

  • The display list is the only render path, and toDisplayList is public. The old per-node SVG render was deleted.
  • The engine runs in plain Node with no DOM. Five specs ran with no source change (bars, a 1,000-point scatter, lines with a legend, a polar chart, a geo map).
  • A painter with no DOM exists: displayListToSVG in gofish-ir returns an SVG string.
  • Only 5 of 165 engine files import SolidJS.
  • The engine already asks its host questions through one interface, DeriveBridge.call(lambdaId, rows, refs). Python callbacks use it.

What is not true yet:

  • Text is guessed without a browser. With no canvas, width is 0.6 em per character. Nothing reports this, so a headless layout is silently different.
  • Text items do not record the size layout assumed. A painter with another font draws text that disagrees with its box.
  • Image natural size is read from the DOM.
  • Ids come from a global counter, so two renders of one spec give different ids.
  • The display list is pixels. Coords are already baked into paths, colors are resolved, and there is one item per mark. No columns, no transforms.
  • Coords are a closed set. There is no inverse, and code tests type === "linear" in six files. Coord.geo could live in another package in JS but could not cross to Python.
  • Python cannot run the engine. to_svg() and save() need a widget that has been displayed in a notebook.

Step 1: the engine as a pure function

The engine becomes (spec, size, host answers) -> display list, with nothing read from the environment behind its back.

What changes for a user

Nothing in a browser. In Node:

import { chart, spread, rect } from "gofish-graphics";
import { displayListToSVG } from "gofish-ir";

const doc = await chart(data)
  .flow(spread({ by: "month", dir: "x" }))
  .mark(rect({ h: "count", fill: "weather" }))
  .toDisplayList({ w: 640, h: 400, fonts: [interRegular] }); // NEW option

const svg = displayListToSVG(doc);

And a painter becomes a render option, with SVG as the written default: 

chart(data).flow(...).mark(...).render(container, { w: 640, h: 400, painter: Painter.svg() }); // NEW

The pieces

  1. Text measurement is passed in. All measuring already goes through one function, estimateTextDimensions. The spike's patch is 7 lines. The proper version is a per-render option, not a global. Two spellings are possible. A function, measureText(text, font) -> { width, ascent, descent }, is the smallest interface and what a host implements. A list of font files, fonts, is what a user of a headless host wants to say, and it is what Satori, resvg and vl-convert take. I lean to both at their own level: the engine takes the function, and the Node and Python hosts take fonts and build the function.
  2. Headless hosts ship one default font. The current default family is system-ui, which has no fixed meaning outside a browser. On macOS it is a variable font that resvg cannot draw at all. vl-convert bundles Liberation Sans for this reason.
  3. No silent guess. Without a measurer, the engine should fail loudly or use a named estimate the user chose. Today it guesses and says nothing.
  4. Text items record width, ascent and descent. A painter then knows the box layout assumed, whatever font it draws with.
  5. Image size is a host answer of the same kind as text size.
  6. Ids are stable, made from the mark's key path, not a counter. A painter that updates a picture in place, and a progressive source that sends many answers, both need this.
  7. The engine can be imported without SolidJS. Move gofish(), render and the DOM export code out of gofish.tsx into the SVG painter, and remove the JSX type from the render options.
  8. A painter draws a closed set of item kinds. The display list has seven: rect, ellipse, path, text, image, group, composite. Makie has kept its backend contract at 11 primitive plot types for about six years, adding one. The lesson is to keep this set small and closed, and to add marks above it.

Evidence from the spike

Spec Time in Node Display list size Pixels that differ from the browser, with a fontkit measurer
Stacked bars 55 ms 184 KiB 1.3%
Scatter, 1,000 points 105 ms 274 KiB 0.5%
Lines with a legend 25 ms 21 KiB 0.4%
Polar 6 ms 19 KiB 1.5%
Geo map 1.9 s 5 MB 0%

Browser render and Node render of the same spec:

The same pair for scatter, lines, polar and the geo map, with the pixels that differ

Text width is the whole difference. opentype.js reads the macOS system font 5 to 15% narrow, because Chrome applies the font's optical-size axis and opentype.js does not. fontkit with that axis set matches Chrome at 12 px. This is the reason for piece 2: a bundled, non-variable default font removes the question.

The geo map is slow and large because every coastline becomes a long path string. That is a cost of the pixel display list, discussed in fork 1.

Step 2: the engine inside Python

The Python package runs the same engine in the kernel process, so a plain script can make a picture and a painter that lives in Python can draw it.

What changes for a user

c = chart(df).flow(spread(by="month", dir="x")).mark(rect(h="count", fill="weather"))

c.save("bars.svg")  # works in a plain script; today it needs a displayed widget
c.save("bars.png")  # NEW
doc = c.to_display_list(w=640, h=400)  # NEW: the display list as Python data

from gofish_fpl import Painter  # NEW: a painter that lives in the kernel

c.render(painter=Painter.pygfx())

In a notebook, c alone still shows the widget, drawn in the browser as today.

Evidence from the spike

  • The engine bundles to one file of 892 KiB (323 KiB gzipped).
  • An embedded V8 (the mini-racer package) ran all five specs with the engine unmodified. Cold start is about 0.6 s. Warm runs take 5 to 350 ms, except the geo map at 3 to 5 s.
  • A column of one million float64 values crosses into V8 in about 50 ms as raw bytes, against about 0.6 s as JSON.
  • matplotlib drew all five display lists.
The other four display lists drawn by matplotlib
  • pygfx drew the bars and the scatter offscreen. Layout, axes and legend match the browser. The fills are visibly lighter, probably a color space difference the spike did not fix. Filled paths are not handled, so the polar chart and the map were not tried.

What did not work honestly

A million points worked only through a stand-in. The engine has no way to return a scale, so the spike laid out a four-row chart at the column's extents and recovered the data-to-pixel transform from where those four rows landed. pygfx then drew a million points from numpy in 3.2 s.

The picture is right, and it is the picture we want: the axes and legend are GoFish's, and the points never left numpy. But the method is a trick that breaks for any coord that is not affine. Doing it properly is fork 1.

A bug found on the way

Serialize.toJSON writes Coord.geo as { dataWindow, domain }, not { projection, lon, lat }, so a geo spec does not survive a round trip through the IR. The spike rewrote it by hand. Not yet filed.

The extension slots

How each kind of extension is spelled, and what it needs from GoFish. The rule for syntactic sharing is that an extension adds values to things GoFish already has. It never adds a new way to write a visualization.

Slot What a user writes Example from the corpus What GoFish must add
Data type a schema entry H3(), a geometry column with its CRS Types that carry geometry: a point for scatter({ at }), a ring for polygon
Source the data argument of chart array(movie, dims=...), csv(url), read_parquet(...) A source interface. Today data is rows in memory
Coord coord= at a chart or layer EPSG codes in Coord.geo Declared properties in place of type === "linear", an inverse, registration
Strategy member Family.member() Curve.geodesic(), Bin.h3() Function strategies (#1101, one extension model for strategy families)
Mark a call inside .mark() or layer basemap("carto-positron") Nothing in JS: a mark that composes existing marks already works, as GoTree shows
Painter a .render(...) option Painter.deckgl(), Painter.pygfx() Step 1

Three points about this table.

Most extensions should be compositions, not new primitives. GoTree is the precedent: it adds no node kind and no IR entry, only functions that return GoFish. The principles page says a feature that cannot desugar into the core should be rethought. So this proposal does not offer a public way to write a new layout or lowering kind. ggplot2 shows the cost of the other choice: extensions subclass its internal objects, and its 4.0.0 release broke 77 Bioconductor packages.

A domain package must add a thing once, not once per painter. GeoViews re-subclasses every plot class for each backend, so it maintains a grid of elements by backends. Because every GoFish mark lowers to the same seven item kinds, a new mark works with every painter for free. This is the main reason to keep the painter contract closed.

The split with a geo library follows sf and ggplot2. sf does the coordinate reference system work, the graticules and the geometry. ggplot2 keeps scales, guides and layout. A GoFish geo package would keep GeoArrow, projections, tiles and the deck.gl painter. GoFish supplies the color scale, the legend, layering, selection, and composition with other visualizations.

Three forks

These are the places where I do not think the answer is clear. Each is shown at the example where it bites.

Fork 1. What the display list carries for large data

It bites at the million-point scatter above and at the movie example (40 x 40 x 60 = 96,000 rect rows for a tiny movie; a real one has 1e8).

Today the display list is one item per mark, in pixels. That cannot carry a million points, and the engine cannot build them anyway.

(a) Leave it. Painters draw what the engine can lay out, which is browser-sized data. A pygfx or deck.gl painter then gives a domain library GoFish's layout, axes and legends, but none of its own speed. Cost: nothing to build. It does not make the partner's case.

(b) Record each chart's box and its data-to-pixel transform in the display list. A painter can then draw its own arrays into the plot box, as the spike did by hand. Cost: small (the affine version exists inside the interaction code already). It is a shortcut: it only works for affine coords, and the points are outside the display list, so selectAll, labels and hit testing cannot see them.

(c) A column item. One display item stands for many marks: a shape kind, references to columns for each channel, and a declared transform. This is the mark table from the scaling proposal, surfaced in the display list. A painter that cannot draw it asks the core to expand it into plain items, so the SVG painter needs no change and the item is sugar over what exists. deck.gl's binary attributes and Makie's primitives both work this way. Cost: it depends on the column engine in the scaling proposal, which is unsigned and large, and on coords that can describe themselves (for a GPU painter, a coord given only as a JavaScript function cannot run in a shader).

My lean: (c) is the destination, and steps 1 and 2 do not depend on it. Take (b) only if a partner wants to start building before (c) exists, and declare it as a shortcut.

Fork 2. Which JavaScript runtime the Python package embeds

It bites at c.save("bars.png") in a plain script.

Runtime Ran Cold start Size Note
mini-racer (V8) 5 of 5, engine unmodified 0.6 s 61 MB installed (wheel about 20 MB) Works today from PyPI
QuickJS 3 of 5, with polyfills not measured 2.3 MB No Intl, which time axes need. Ran out of memory on the map
Node subprocess 5 of 5 0.12 s none The user must have node installed
Our own wheel with Deno (what vl-convert does) not tried not measured about 30 MB We would build and ship wheels per platform

My lean: mini-racer, as an optional extra (pip install "gofish-graphics[headless]"), so the notebook path stays light. A Node subprocess is what issue #577 (headless SVG rendering in Node) proposed. It is faster to start, but "install Node first" is a poor answer for the Python scientists who are the 1.0 audience. I would not build our own wheel until mini-racer fails us.

Fork 3. How an extension's constructs reach Python

It bites at from gofish_geo import basemap.

from gofish_geo import basemap, Painter  # NEW

In JavaScript an extension is easy: a function that returns GoFish. In Python it is not. GoTree's Python side is a second implementation of 490 lines, marked as a shortcut for #1163 (how an extension package crosses to Python), with 40 parity stories to stop the two from drifting.

(a) Write each extension twice, as GoTree does. Cost: every domain package pays this, and it is the opposite of sharing work.

(b) Registration. The package declares its constructs in a descriptor, as core constructs are declared today, and registers a JavaScript factory under a name. The Python wrapper is generated from the descriptor. The IR carries the construct by name, and the JavaScript side expands it. Step 2 makes this practical: the kernel can load the package's JavaScript into the embedded runtime, and the widget can load the same file. Cost: a registration API in two packages, a generator that runs per package, and a rule for versions.

(c) Python-first extensions. A Python package composes Python combinators and never ships JavaScript. Cost: nothing new to build, but the extension does not exist for JavaScript users, and anything that needs code in the engine (a projection, a tile source) cannot be written this way.

My lean: (b). It is #1163 and #692 (public defineMark and defineOperator with registration) answered together, and it is the piece that decides whether lonboard's author, who works in Python and Rust, could ship one package.

What the three consumers would own

Keeps Gets from GoFish Needs beyond steps 1 and 2
lonboard GeoArrow and GeoParquet, CRS, projections, tiles, the deck.gl painter Color scales and legends, linked views without hand-written observers, a map beside a histogram Fork 1 (c) for its speed, open coords, registration
fastplotlib Arrays with named dims, video decoding, the pygfx painter, GPU colormaps A declarative front end, legends (its issue 403 is open), layout of panels, overlays in one data space Fork 1 for its speed, Python inputs, the scale-sharing wall fixed
A progressive library Chunk order, estimators, error bounds, the scheduler Every GoFish visualization, not a few bespoke ones A source that answers more than once, stable ids, fixed bins and declared domains

On progressive sources: the ProVega paper (arXiv 2604.02096, a Vega-Lite extension for progressive loading) says "ProgressiVis has no knowledge of marks or encodings". A GoFish spec's data part (the by keys, the bins, the channel aggregates) is what such a library could run in pieces. The example render shows what must be declared for the picture to stay still while it fills in: the color domain moved from 7 to 419 across frames, and the bins followed the data seen so far.

Precedent

Makie

What an extension author writes
A recipe that calls other plots, or a conversion of a data type
What the core keeps
11 primitive plot types that each of four backends draws
Lesson
A small closed painter contract lasts. Makie also paid for a breaking rewrite to make updates lazy

ggplot2

What an extension author writes
A subclass of an internal Stat, Geom or Coord
What the core keeps
Scales, guides, layout, one renderer
Lesson
Do not expose internals. Its own guide calls the object system a "historical accident"

ggplot2 with sf

What an extension author writes
sf does CRS, graticules, geometry
What the core keeps
ggplot2 keeps the rest
Lesson
The split to copy for geo

HoloViews, GeoViews

What an extension author writes
A plot class per element per backend
What the core keeps
Elements as data containers
Lesson
The grid to avoid

vl-convert

What an extension author writes
Nothing; it runs Vega unchanged in an embedded Deno
What the core keeps
Its own text shaping and fonts in version 2
Lesson
Text measurement belongs to the core, not to the painter

deck.gl

What an extension author writes
A layer with accessors, or binary column attributes
What the core keeps
The GPU pipeline
Lesson
Columns go by reference, never as per-row objects

Observable Plot

What an extension author writes
A mark, with a note on whether it handles projections
What the core keeps
Scales and projection
Lesson
Each mark says whether a projection bends it or only moves it

Who benefits

The rewritten programs are about as long as the originals. Line count is not the benefit. The benefit is in what the originals cannot do at all, and it falls unevenly.

Who gains

Who What they gain What it depends on
GoFish's own Python users A plain script can save an SVG or a PNG, with no notebook. This is already on the 1.0 list Step 2 only. No partner, no fork
People whose work crosses domains One grammar for views that today come from three libraries. The views share scales and legends, and they link with a filter The scale wall fixed, then the painter slot
Authors of new domain libraries They do not build legends, axes, layout, widgets or export. They write the column types, sources and painter for their domain Registration (fork 3)
Authors of existing domain libraries The parts they have not built. Neither lonboard nor fastplotlib has legends, and linking two lonboard maps takes hand-written observer callbacks Fork 1 for their speed, and their own wish to depend on GoFish
Progressive libraries Every GoFish visualization, in place of a few views written by hand. ProgressiVis computes but knows nothing about marks A source that answers more than once

The second row is the strongest case in the long run. A neuroscientist with a movie, traces, a histogram and a brain map uses several libraries today, each with its own colormap, its own legend and its own idea of selection. The movie example in the corpus is this case in small: the frame, the regions, the traces and the time markers are one spec, and one slider drives all of them.

New libraries gain more than existing ones. lonboard and fastplotlib have already paid for most of what GoFish would supply. Someone starting a genomics library today has not.

Who does not gain

  • A user who wants one map quickly. viz(gdf) is shorter than any GoFish spec, and it stays that way.
  • Anyone who needs the domain library's speed today. Until fork 1 is done, a GoFish painter draws browser-sized data only.
  • Anyone who needs what GoFish has no model for. A 3D camera with pitch and bearing, or changing GPU buffers at frame rate, are two examples from the corpus.

Two weak points in the case

The benefit across domains depends on core work, not on extensions. Five of the nine examples hit the wall where one render has one set of scales. Until that is fixed, the composed version looks worse than the separate libraries do: in the movie example the traces are squashed, because their panel took the image's y range.

The benefit to partners is a guess. Neither author has asked for this. Depending on a young library is a real cost to them, and the design assumes they would accept it.

So the work is ordered by who is sure to benefit.

Order of work

  1. Step 1. Text measurer as a render option, text metrics on text items, image size as a host answer, stable ids, an engine import with no SolidJS, the geo toJSON fix. This closes most of #577 and #814 (export a text measurement utility) and prepares #1337 (one SVG backend).
  2. Step 2. The Python headless host: save and to_svg in plain scripts, to_display_list, and a painter protocol in Python with matplotlib as the reference painter. This closes the rest of #577 and #578 (PNG export). Steps 1 and 2 serve GoFish's own users and need no partner.
  3. Fix the scale wall. Sibling panels in one render need their own color scale and their own position domains when their data differs.
  4. Build one visualization that crosses domains. A map linked to a histogram, with shared legends, is a good first one. No single library can draw it today. This is what to show the lonboard and fastplotlib authors, before building anything for them.
  5. Ask the authors. Would they build on this, and what would they refuse to give up?
  6. Investigate the rest in parallel.
    • Run capture-diff over the whole gallery with the bundled-font measurer against the browser, to learn how far headless layouts move.
    • Prototype fork 1 (c) on one mark: a scatter as a column item, drawn by deck.gl's binary attributes.
    • Check that mini-racer wheels and every engine dependency work on Windows and Linux.
